analysis.one_liner: Bars internet providers from sharing subscribers' personal information without their written consent.
analysis.headline: The bill never left a House subcommittee, and no vote was ever taken before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This 1996 bill would have required internet service providers and online services to get a subscriber's signed, informed written consent before sharing that subscriber's personal information with anyone else. Subscribers could revoke consent at any time, see and correct the information a service kept about them, find out who received it, and never be charged a fee for asking. The Federal Trade Commission could investigate violations and order them stopped, and subscribers could sue. The bill was referred to a House Commerce subcommittee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet and online service subscribers, who would gain control over whether companies could sell or hand off their personal information, plus a right to see and correct the records kept about them [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Providers could not disclose a subscriber's personally identifiable information to any third party without the subscriber's prior informed written consent, and the subscriber could revoke that consent at any time [S3].

At a subscriber's request, the service had to show the subscriber the personal information it held, let the subscriber verify and correct errors, and name the third parties who had received it — all free of charge [S3].
The Federal Trade Commission could investigate services for violations and issue cease-and-desist orders, and an aggrieved subscriber could sue for relief in civil court [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Internet service providers and online services, which would lose the ability to freely use or sell subscriber data, and any marketers who relied on receiving it.

drawbacks.text: In 1996, the commercial internet was in its infancy; a consent-and-disclosure regime written that early could have imposed paperwork and compliance costs on a young industry, and the bill's definition of an interactive computer service (access via modem) would have needed constant rewriting as technology changed [S3].

The bill required written, signed consent for each disclosure, a rigid standard that even privacy advocates might find unworkable today; it offered no exceptions for ordinary operational data sharing such as billing or fraud prevention [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections — consent before data sharing, access to and correction of one's own records, and FTC enforcement — are the same core principles Congress and states spent the following decades debating without enacting federally. The compliance burden on 1996-era providers was real but modest, and the bill's narrow, modem-era definitions show the difficulty of legislating on a fast-moving technology. On balance, the privacy gains for ordinary subscribers outweighed the costs, which is why its failure looks like a missed early opportunity.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote before the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Vento introduced the bill on September 18, 1996, in the final months of the 104th Congress [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Commerce; a week later it went to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials, and the record shows no further action [S5].
Six members cosponsored the bill — five Democrats and one Independent [S4].
Congress adjourned on January 3, 1997, and the bill died without ever reaching the House floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet service providers and online services came out ahead, keeping their freedom to use and sell subscriber personal information without consent — a practice the bill would have curtailed. Ordinary subscribers gained nothing, and no federal baseline for online privacy existed at all for years afterward.

for.name: Rep. Bruce Vento
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no opposition is recorded; the bill simply died in subcommittee with six cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents, so no partisan split can be measured [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Internet service providers and online services
industries.note: The bill would have barred them from disclosing subscriber personal information without signed consent and forced them to give subscribers access to and correction of their own records [S3]. Their interest in keeping subscriber data freely usable ran directly against subscribers' privacy.

industries.industry: Direct marketers and early data brokers
industries.note: Any business buying personally identifiable subscriber information from online services would have lost that supply unless the subscriber signed off, and would have been named to the subscriber on request [S3].
